items.title: Dan Morgenstern interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 9, 2013
items.q: I was a Wallace — Henry Wallace was running for president.

ctx.x: Well you must have been on your way to becoming pretty hip yourself, even maybe you didn’t even realize it.

I had no thoughts at that time of becoming in any way professionally involved in the music, but I was — it was like 52nd Street was in its final stages, but it was still alive and it was no small thing to have Sidney Bechet at Jimmy Ryan’s and across the street maybe Charlie Parker if you were lucky and he was in town. And, you know, Billie Holiday at the Onyx Club. So there was still a lot going on. And this was, you know, still a vibrant time. There was downtown on weekends, there was the Stuyvesant Casino in…

not much more than a glorified messenger but I got to meet a lot of people and actually was talked into running for office at the American Newspaper Guild, a pretty left wing thing. I was a Wallace — Henry Wallace was running for president. That was that famous election when Truman — Truman and Dewey. And it was a great experience because I was working at Time Inc. I was at a nerve center there on election night, which was a studio where they were broadcasting, and there was a guy named H.V. Kaltenborn, who was —…

items.title: Dan Morgenstern — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I got involved with the Progressive Party, rang doorbells for Henry Wallace, and went to a couple of meetings

ctx.x: We’re at the point where you’ve come to the United States. The first thing I want to ask you about is, now you’re united with your father and how many years had it

I had last seen my father – we managed – he couldn’t get into Denmark, and my mother and I couldn’t get into France, which was probably a good thing, considering what happened later. But it was possible for my mother and me to visit my father in Paris in the spring of 1939 for about two weeks. That was the last time I had seen him. So it was eight years – almost exactly eight years. That’s a long time developmentally. When I’d last seen him, I was pre-teen. When I saw him again, I was in my late teens, a…

brother was killed in World War I. Another brother was a harmless, nice man, who was a tailor. But the Germans killed him in Buchenwald. When my father, after the war, found out in more detail about all the things that have happened – his mother and sister were first taken to Theresienstadt, which was, as we know, that concentration camp that the Germans had in Czechoslovakia, which was like – where they weren’t killing people. It wasn’t an extermination camp. But most people who were there were eventually…
